name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: OXO Good Grips
items.fact: In 1990 Sam Farber launched kitchen tools with thick, soft, rubbery handles after he saw his wife, who had arthritis, struggle with an ordinary vegetable peeler. Now everyone uses them.

items.name: The Xbox Adaptive Controller
items.fact: In 2018 Microsoft launched a games controller with two huge buttons and many sockets, so that players who can't use a normal controller can plug in switches, pedals or joysticks.

items.name: Banknotes you can feel
items.fact: After a blind teenager, Connor McLeod, campaigned for it, Australia's new banknotes from 2016 have small raised bumps on the edge, so blind people can tell the notes apart.

items.name: Shoes without laces
items.fact: Nike's FlyEase shoes, which you can put on and close with one hand, were inspired by a letter from Matthew Walzer, a teenager with cerebral palsy who couldn't tie his laces.

items.name: Clothes with magnets
items.fact: Tommy Hilfiger makes adaptive clothing for disabled people: shirts and trousers that close with magnets instead of buttons, and wider openings that make it easier to get dressed.

items.name: Be My Eyes
items.fact: Be My Eyes, a Danish app launched in 2015, connects blind people by video call with sighted volunteers, who help with things like reading labels. Millions of volunteers have signed up.

items.name: A colour code for colour-blind people
items.fact: Portuguese designer Miguel Neiva created ColorADD, a set of simple symbols for colours. It is used on things like school pencils, maps and hospital labels so colour-blind people can identify colours.

items.name: The steady spoon
items.fact: Liftware makes a spoon with a handle full of sensors and small motors. It moves against the shaking of the hand, so people with a tremor spill much less food.

items.name: The first TV captions
items.fact: The first TV programme with captions for deaf viewers in the USA was a cooking show, Julia Child's The French Chef, in 1972.

items.name: Dropped kerbs
items.fact: In the 1970s, disabled activists in Berkeley, California, pushed for small slopes in kerbs for wheelchairs. They turned out to help everyone: people with pushchairs, suitcases and bikes too.

fakes.name: The talking trolley
fakes.fact: A Swedish supermarket chain fitted some trolleys with a small scanner that reads the price labels aloud to blind shoppers through a speaker in the handle.

fakes.name: The vibrating door handle
fakes.fact: Danish designers made hotel door handles that vibrate gently when the door locks, so that deaf guests know their room is closed.

fakes.name: The humming zebra crossing
fakes.fact: Spanish engineers built a zebra crossing in Valencia whose stripes light up and hum while a wheelchair user is crossing, so drivers wait longer.

fakes.name: The cooling fork
fakes.fact: An Italian designer made a fork with a tiny fan in the handle that cools hot food, for people who find it hard to blow on their food.

fakes.name: Puzzles that smell
fakes.fact: A Canadian toy company makes jigsaw puzzles in which every piece has a different smell, so that blind children can find the pieces that fit.

fakes.name: Lifts that speak dialect
fakes.fact: Some lifts in Zurich announce the floors in Swiss German dialect, after older residents said they found the standard German voice hard to follow.

fakes.name: The flashing umbrella
fakes.fact: An Irish start-up makes umbrellas for blind people with a small light in the tip that flashes when they step into the road, so drivers see them in the rain.

fakes.name: Scented bus stops
fakes.fact: A Portuguese city gave each bus stop on one line a different smell from a small dispenser, so that blind passengers could tell which stop they had reached.

fakes.name: The warm keypad
fakes.fact: A Dutch company makes a phone whose keys get slightly warmer the longer you press them, so people with poor eyesight know a key has been pressed.

fakes.name: The kettle that weighs
fakes.fact: A British kettle for blind people weighs the water inside and says aloud how many cups it will make, so nobody overfills it.
